newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania unveils "work, sweat and austerity" steps.
newsitem.headline: Romania unveils "work, sweat and austerity" steps.

text.p: Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea has unveiled tough reforms, promising only "work, sweat and austerity" to put his country's economy on a market footing, with renewed support from international lenders.
Ciorbea, flanked by key coalition government ministers, detailed what he called "a programme designed to save the national economy" during a news conference late on Monday.

"The core of this programme will be radical reform of production, consumption, monetary, currency and capital markets and stimulation of free initiative," he said of sweeping reforms drafted together with International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank experts.
The package also included social protection steps aimed at cushioning the impact of liberalisation of prices, including meat, milk, bread and energy, on the most disadvantaged citizens.

Ciorbea urged fellow Romanians to understand the necessity of the painful reforms, which he said would further dent their living standards and push many workers into unemployment as the government streamlines loss-making communist-era industries.
Stepping up privatisation of state industries and of the banking sectors would also take centre stage, he said.
"By end-1997, we must put a total of 3,600 companies into private hands, accounting for 69 percent of the total number of companies up for privatisation," Ciorbea said.

"I can only promise you work, sweat and austerity," he said, paraphrasing the prophesy by Britain's World War Two Prime Minister Winston Churchill to his fellow countrymen of future "blood, sweat and tears".

"We are the generation which has the chance to save Romania," added Ciorbea, who earned his reputation as a no-nonsense labour leader during hard-fought negotiations with previous post-communist governments.
His coalition cabinet faces the difficult task of keeping trade unions at bay, while bringing bulging deficits and inflation under control.

Bucharest is seeking around $1 billion in new loans from the IMF and World Bank. Both lenders suspended credits for Romania last year over foreign currency market curbs and overspending by the former leftists in an election year.
"We cannot succeed on our own," said Ciorbea, whose centrist coalition government came in after ex-communists were removed from office during elections last November.
The government had negotiated "tooth and nail" with IMF, World Bank and European Union experts to achieve accords on financing for the reform programme, he said, but gave no details.
Romania expected a first tranche of a new 12-month stand-by loan accord negotiated with the Fund to come in by April, Ciorbea said, without quoting figures.
The government would submit to parliament up to 90 bills, aiming to bring existing laws in line with European standards, and to create facilities to attract foreign investors.
"We count on a massive inflow of direct foreign investments this year. We had been starved of this kind of investments," Ciorbea said.
Romania, eastern Europe's second-largest market after Poland, has seen only a fraction of the foreign investment poured into more advanced ex-communist neighbours.

"I know how humiliated we felt when in the race for the third millennium, we saw the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovenia and Poland race past us," said Ciorbea. He pledged swiftly to bridge that development gap.
